title: Sigara böreği
subtitle: Turkish cheese-filled cigarette pastries
excerpt: Sigara boregi are slim rolled pastries filled with salty white cheese and herbs, fried until shatteringly crisp. They are named for their resemblance to cigarettes and are one of the most compelling snacks in the Turkish repertoire. A batch disappears almost instantly.
sourceNotes: A fixture at Turkish pastry shops, wedding tables, and home mezze spreads. The filling is classically white cheese (feta or akawi) with parsley; mint is sometimes added.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked on a tray, then bag. Fry from frozen, allowing an extra minute or two.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and freeze half for later.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Form and refrigerate up to 4 hours ahead. Cover with damp kitchen paper to prevent the filo drying out.

content.text: Sigara boregi are one of those things that look impressive but take less time than you expect. A strip of filo, a spoonful of cheese, a roll and a seal: the process repeats itself until you have a plate of slim, tightly wound pastries ready for the pan.
Frying gives them their defining texture: the outside shatters into thousands of tiny crisp shards while the inside stays molten and salty. Baking works but does not give the same result.

Keep the filo covered with a damp cloth while you work; it dries out within minutes and becomes brittle and unworkable. Work quickly and seal each roll with a dab of water or the egg mixture before setting aside.

items.prepNote: cut in half to give 16 rectangles
crumbled (or use any salty white cheese)

content.text: Make the filling and prepare the filo

Combine the crumbled feta, parsley, mint if using, egg, and black pepper in a bowl and mix well. Taste; the feta may be salty enough without adding more salt. Cut the filo sheets in half lengthways to give strips about 12 cm by 30 cm. Keep covered with a damp cloth.

Place a strip of filo on a clean surface with the short end nearest you. Spoon a heaped tablespoon of filling in a narrow sausage shape across the bottom of the strip, leaving a 1 cm gap at each side. Fold the bottom edge up over the filling, fold in the sides, and roll up tightly toward the top. Brush the final edge with a little beaten egg to seal. Set seam-side down on a tray. Repeat with all strips.

Heat the olive oil in the frying pan over medium heat until a small piece of filo sizzles immediately when dropped in. Fry the pastries in batches, seam-side down first, for about 2 minutes per side until golden all over. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper. Serve immediately; they lose their crispness quickly.

rows.cause: Dried out or rolled too tightly
rows.fix: Keep filo covered at all times. If a sheet tears, use two layers together.
Make sure the final edge is sealed with egg and press firmly. Fry seam-side down first.

rows.symptom: Oil soaked into the pastry and greasy result
rows.fix: Test the oil temperature before frying. It must sizzle immediately on contact; oil that is too cool leads to greasy pastry.

content.text: Replace half the feta with mashed potato for a softer, less salty filling. Spinach and feta is a popular alternative: squeeze dry, chopped frozen spinach mixed into the cheese filling. For a meat version, replace the cheese with the spiced lamb filling from dolma biber.
Form the pastries up to 4 hours ahead and cover with a damp cloth in the fridge. Fry just before serving. For longer storage, freeze the uncooked pastries and fry directly from frozen.

Sigara boregi are sold at Turkish patisseries and at the pastry counter of any good lokanta. They are a standard part of mezze spreads, appear on wedding buffets, and are made at home as a treat. The shape is consistent but the filling varies from region to region and family to family.
